claims_disputed.claim: The quality checker detects seeded requirement defects
claims_disputed.reason: Table III's two perfect rows are rule self-tests. The escape-clause mutant appends ', where possible and as appropriate', and §III-B lists 'as appropriate' verbatim as a rule term. The missing-criteria mutant deletes the field that the rule checks for. The only structurally different defect, a packed second 'shall' clause, scored 0/36, and vague terms scored 17/36. There is no sample of real-world defective requirements and no comparison with human review, so 'detects seeded defects' holds only for the phrases the rules enumerate.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The paper does more than mention spec-first work. §IV-C2 reports that VNVSpec has been developed against its own committed self-spec since v0.1.0, assessed in CI on every commit, with a stated policy that a change breaking self-assessment is rolled back rather than the spec. That is the pattern in use, without an isolating comparison, which is 'introduces'. The agent variant remains proposal-only.

missed_issues: auto_trace() (§III-D) creates 'verifies' edges from any requirement-ID mention in test names, docstrings or comments. A comment mention therefore counts as verification evidence even when the test asserts nothing about the requirement. Link precision is never measured, which matters for P42's 'verified links'.

Verdict roll-up treats a passing linked test as passing evidence for the requirement (§III-E). Nothing checks that the test exercises the requirement's acceptance criterion. The self-spec's 'every requirement passing' (§IV-C2) therefore measures tagging plus a green suite, not requirement satisfaction.

The checker emits 62 warnings on the authors' own 36 requirements and 186 on the 116 catalog requirements, roughly 1.6 to 1.7 warnings per requirement, all advisory (§IV-C5). Warning precision is not measured, so whether developers would act on or ignore these warnings is unknown.

The Java path is asserted, not shown. The 5,000-case JUnit XML file (§IV-C4) is synthetic, and the only foreign-runner example is Jest with a custom jest-junit property hook (Listing 3). How a requirement ID reaches Surefire or Gradle JUnit 5 XML is not demonstrated.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats and with the review's framing: a released, cheaply measured tool with no evidence that it improves traceability, effort or audit outcomes, and an agent extension that is future work. I score rigor one point lower because the only non-runtime experiment largely re-runs the checker's own rule list. I lower the quality-checker claim to weak for the same reason; its informative content is the negative 0/36 on compound requirements. I upgrade P14 to introduces because the authors do practise spec-first development on the tool itself. The review's applicability (requirement IDs on JUnit tests, untested means inconclusive, distinct exit codes) is a fair reading, but it is established requirements-as-code practice (Doorstop, Sphinx-needs, BDD tags), and the paper provides no evidence beyond its existence.
